chief_complaint: painful mouth sores and blisters on palms and soles
hpi_details: 4-year-old girl is brought in by her parent with painful mouth sores and blisters on her palms and soles that began 2 days ago. She has a low-grade fever and is drinking less because swallowing hurts.
ideas: The mother thinks her daughter caught chickenpox or an unusual viral bug from one of her preschool classmates.
concerns: She is worried that her daughter will get severely dehydrated because she cries and refuses to drink any fluids.
expectations: She hopes to get a numbing mouth medicine so her child can drink comfortably and a doctor's note for preschool.
social_hx: Attends preschool; several classmates have had similar symptoms.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Hand, foot, and mouth disease evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hand, foot, and mouth disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Hand Foot and Mouth Disease: Supportive pain control (ibuprofen/acetaminophen), cold liquids, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painful mouth sores and blisters on palms and soles
Key HPI features: A 4-year-old girl has 2 days of painful oral sores and palm/sole blisters with low-grade fever and reduced drinking because swallowing hurts.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Hand Foot and Mouth Disease.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hand, foot, and mouth disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Herpangina without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Poor oral intake from mouth pain leading to dehydration.
management_principles: Plan for Hand Foot and Mouth Disease: Supportive care with weight-based acetaminophen or ibuprofen when appropriate, plus cold liquids; avoid aspirin and oral topical anesthetics
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) Clinical Practice Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of painful mouth sores and blisters on palms and soles. HPI: hand foot and mouth disease.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Hand Foot and Mouth Disease.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Hand Foot and Mouth Disease.
reference_soap.plan: Supportive care with weight-based acetaminophen or ibuprofen when appropriate and cold liquids. Avoid aspirin and oral topical anesthetics. Seek urgent care for signs of dehydration, lethargy, breathing difficulty, or inability to drink.

Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Hand Foot and Mouth Disease

teaching.one_liner: Patient with painful mouth sores and blisters on the palms and soles.

must_ask.say: Can you describe the mouth sores — where are they and how painful?

must_ask.objective: Ask about the rash on hands and feet
must_ask.say: Are there blisters or spots on her palms and soles?

must_ask.objective: Assess oral intake given mouth pain
must_ask.say: Is she able to eat or drink despite the mouth pain?

must_ask.objective: Ask about fever and contact with other sick children
must_ask.say: Has she had a fever, and has she been around other children with similar symptoms?
This is viral and will resolve on its own — we'll focus on pain control and cold liquids to keep her comfortable and hydrated.

history.answer: My daughter has painful sores inside her mouth, and small blisters broke out on her hands and feet two days ago.
It began two days ago with a low fever and fussiness, and then the mouth sores and the bumps on her hands and feet appeared yesterday.
The sores are inside her cheeks and tongue, and the little blisters are scattered on the palms of her hands, the soles of her feet, and a few on her bottom.
They look like tiny reddish spots and small oval gray-white water blisters, about the size of sesame seeds, with a thin red circle around them.
She cries that her mouth hurts a lot, especially when she tries to swallow, but the bumps on her hands and feet don't seem to itch or bother her much.
No, they have stayed in the exact same spots since they broke out rather than fading and moving around.
No, she has never had an illness or blistery rash like this before.
She had a mild fever around 37.8 degrees Celsius when this started two days ago, but no severe chills or shaking.
Yes, she has several small shallow sores inside her cheeks and tongue, and she cries and points to her mouth whenever she tries to eat.
No, her eyes look clear without any redness or drainage, and there are no sores in her private area.
No, her skin is not peeling off at all, and there are no dark purple spots or bruises anywhere.
No, her lips, tongue, and face are not swollen, and she is breathing easily and comfortably.
She is refusing all solid food and will only take small sips of cold water or milk because swallowing hurts so much.
She has only peed twice today, and her urine was a bit darker yellow than usual, but she still makes tears when she cries.
She is fussier than usual and tired from not sleeping well, but she still makes eye contact, walks around, and plays with her toys.
She had a slightly runny nose the first day, but no persistent cough, vomiting, or diarrhea.
No, her joints are not swollen or painful, and her fingernails and toenails look completely normal.
We haven't put any creams or ointments on the blisters, but we gave her children's acetaminophen once for the fever yesterday.
She hasn't started any antibiotics, anti-seizure drugs, or other new medications recently.
No, she hasn't eaten any new foods, and we haven't changed her soap, bath wash, or laundry detergent.
No, she hasn't had any bug bites, and we haven't gone hiking, visited public pools, or traveled out of town.
She goes to preschool on weekdays, and her teacher said yesterday that two other children in her classroom came down with the same kind of blisters.
No one else in our house has fever, mouth sores, or any rash right now.
I thought maybe she caught chickenpox or some kind of bug that's been going around her preschool class.
I'm really scared she's going to get dehydrated because she cries and pushes her cup away whenever I try to give her water.
I'm hoping you can give us a soothing mouth spray so she can drink fluids, and a note letting the preschool know when she can go back.
She has always been healthy with no chronic medical problems or kidney and heart disease.
She has never had surgery, and she has never been admitted to a hospital.
She does not take any regular medications, just a daily chewable children's multivitamin.
She has no known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
She was born full-term through an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and went home healthy on schedule.
She is growing well along the fiftieth percentile for height and weight, and her pediatrician says she is meeting all milestones.
All of her routine childhood vaccinations are completely up to date according to the schedule.
There is no family history of skin diseases, autoimmune disorders, or recurring mouth sores.

exam.finding: Mildly irritable but alert 4-year-old girl sitting on parent's lap; mucous membranes slightly dry, no respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, heart rate 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, body temperature 37.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Multiple small, shallow, painful ulcers with surrounding erythematous halos on the buccal mucosa and tongue; no tonsillar exudate, pharyngeal pseudomembranes, or gingival bleeding.

Multiple discrete 2 to 3 mm oval gray-white vesicles with thin erythematous rims on the palms, soles, and lateral fingers, and a few small erythematous papules on the buttocks; no crusted lesions, target lesions, or purpura.
Mild bilateral anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, mobile and mildly tender; no supraclavicular or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Conjunctivae clear without discharge, injection, or mucosal ulceration; pupils equal, round, and reactive to light.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender without guarding; no hepatosplenomegaly or palpable masses.
Supple neck with full active and passive flexion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
